title: Improve batcher resilience and KV-cache warmup / scheduler tuning
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Summary: Reduce tail latency and transient failures caused by cold KV cache behavior and scheduler contention under bursty traffic. This work addresses three related pain points: (1) slow first-token latency for infrequently used model routes due to KV cache cold starts, (2) scheduler-driven starvation when many short requests arrive concurrently, and (3) brittle retry/backoff interactions between the continuous batcher and autoscaler that amplify latency spikes.

Background: Over the last two quarters we've seen a recurring pattern in customer dashboards: P95/P99 spikes around regional traffic bursts and after deploys. Investigations tied many incidents to ineffective KV cache warmup and imbalanced kernel scheduling that leaves small requests waiting for large inflight batches. Earlier tickets (ENG-4723, ENG-5821) made progress on batcher API and eviction; this ticket focuses on operational resilience and targeted micro-optimizations with measurable SLO improvements.

Goals:
- Implement an opt-in KV warmup policy for pinned/popular routes that prepopulates prefix/KV entries after cold starts and during low load windows.
- Tune the continuous batcher to prefer low-latency small batches when request-size distribution indicates latency-sensitive traffic.
- Introduce a lightweight scheduler fairness heuristic to prevent small-request starvation and to better interoperate with autoscaler scaling events.
- Add observability (traces + histograms) for cache-hit latency, warmup efficacy, scheduler queue lengths, and preemption occurrences.
- Provide a guarded rollout (feature-flag + canary) and a rollback path if memory/cost deltas exceed thresholds.
acceptance_criteria: KV warmup feature implements prefetch policy and can be toggled per-route via config flag
End-to-end test demonstrates <10ms added overhead for warmup and >70% reduction in first-token cold miss latency in bench harness
Batcher scheduling change reduces P95 latency for 0-64 token requests by >=10% in simulated burst scenario
No increase in OOM incidents in canary region; memory delta <= +6% for typical model footprints
Metrics/traces dashboards added and runbook updated with rollback steps
notes: 2026-02-19: Spike triage — identified correlation between cold KV misses and P99 tail during morning traffic ramp (confirmed by tracing). Assigned Diego to own implementation.
2026-02-24: Spike bench — synthetic workload created (50k reqs/min with 70% short queries). Baseline P95 = 210ms, P99 = 470ms. KV cold-miss rate measured at ~18% during window.
2026-03-02: Design sync with Runtime and Storage teams. Decided on probabilistic prefetch (LRU+hotset sampling) instead of full eager load to limit memory pressure.
2026-03-04: Prototype landed in branch: feature/batcher-kv-warmup. Early microbench shows first-token latency improvement ~12% for targeted routes, memory +3.8%.
2026-03-07: PR opened for scheduler fairness: github.com/redwood/infra/pull/1486. Initial review from Priya and Malik noted potential prioritization inversion; added unit tests for preemption order.

2026-03-09: Canary run in us-west-2 for 24h. Observed P95 reduction for small requests from 210ms -> 182ms (-13%). P99 improved by ~9%. No OOMs; KV hit-rate on warmed routes rose from 12% -> 68% after warmup window.
Follow-ups: document operator knobs, add a 'graceful cooldown' to warmup to avoid noisy oscillation, schedule post-rollout perf regression + cost review.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (spike/prototype): implement sampling-based KV prefetch + metrics (1 week)
Phase 2 (batcher/scheduler): add small-request bias and fairness heuristic; integration tests (2 weeks)
Phase 3 (canary): enable in single region behind feature flag, monitor for 48h (3 days)
Phase 4 (rollout): staged ramp + cost validation; enable by default if metrics safe (1 week)
Phase 5 (cleanup): remove debug knobs and harden unit tests; update runbook
risks: Memory pressure if warmup over-eagerly populates large KV entries
Mis-tuned fairness could reduce overall throughput under heavy sustained load
Interaction with autoscaler could cause oscillation if warmup triggers sudden memory growth
Increased complexity in serving runtime may make debugging harder without improved traces
